slides: Open by making isometry concrete: a plane motion is a matrix plus a translation that preserves every distance. The chapter classifies motions by orientation, determinant, and fixed-set behavior, so the lecture should keep asking what is preserved and what is fixed.

Use the route slide to connect classification and construction. First identify direct and opposite motions through determinants, then explain products of reflections, then isolate glide reflections and midpoint scaffolds, and finally read strip patterns as repeated motion recipes rather than decorative borders.

The matrix classifier is the central visual because one sample triangle can expose all six basic motion types. Pairwise distances remain unchanged, while the signed-area ratio follows the determinant. That makes direct versus opposite motion a measurable fact rather than a visual hunch.

Reflection products turn the classification into a construction language. Intersecting mirrors rotate, parallel mirrors translate, perpendicular mirrors make a half-turn, and two half-turns translate. The residuals near zero tell students that the matrix products match the geometric reading.

A glide reflection is the motion that often confuses learners. It reverses orientation like a reflection, but the slide along the axis removes fixed points. The midpoint trace gives a simple invariant: every point and its image have a midpoint on the glide axis.

The Hjelmslev midpoint scaffold gives a second way to recognize hidden isometries. Pair points on two lines by a consistent motion, then examine the midpoint set. A reflection produces a line of midpoints, while a half-turn collapses all midpoints to the center.

Strip patterns turn small motions into repeated structure. The goal is not to memorize strip names, but to look for generators: translations, vertical mirrors, horizontal mirrors, half-turn centers, and glide reflections. The asymmetric motif keeps the orientation changes visible.

The applied classifier lab asks students to reverse the direction of the chapter. Given a candidate matrix, check orthogonality, determinant, and fixed-set rank before naming the isometry. Reporting the residual is the responsible part: a nearly rigid map is not automatically an isometry.

This synthesis slide connects named motions to construction effects. Same-handed copies with a common shift indicate translation, turned copies around a point indicate rotation, handedness reversal with a fixed line indicates reflection, and handedness reversal with no fixed point indicates glide reflection.

Close by emphasizing the two-column discipline of the chapter. Every motion has a geometric description and an algebraic signature: determinant sign, distance preservation, fixed-set type, and composition behavior. The figures are useful because their matrix checks make that signature auditable.
